Chorzele Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Chorzele, Poland

Not demolished. Chorzele, granted town privileges in 1542, saw Jewish settlement from the late 18th century; population reached 2.6% (1792) growing to 35.4% by 1827 and 57% (2,301) by 1905. WWI-era Russian displacement sent many residents to Przasnysz; postwar Zionist sentiment led about 150 people to emigrate to Israel. A WWII ghetto gradually deported residents to Warsaw, Maków Mazowiecki, Legionowo, Węgrów, and Mława through December 1941, before most reached Treblinka or Auschwitz. This cemetery, established by at least the second half of the 19th century and maintained by a local Chevra Kadisha, held sandstone, fieldstone, concrete, marble, and even terrazzo tombstones. Germans devastated the site during WWII, using matzevot to harden sidewalks; part became an exercise area, another part a German soldiers' burial ground. Locals further destroyed remaining tombstones postwar. A 1989 Social Committee for the Renewal of the Jewish Cemetery, led by Mayor Ludwik Rogowski with local clergy support, initiated cleanup; a 1991 monument by the Association of Jews from Chorzele in Israel used recovered Mostowa Street matzevot, and a 2006 plaque honored Auschwitz survivor Dawid Fiszerung's family.
